questions.q: Which sequence gives the book's tubular/interstitial, glomerular and vascular proportions, respectively?
questions.exp: The renal compartment tree allocates 85% to tubules/interstitium, 10% to glomeruli and 5% to vessels. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which statement handles the bladder-origin line accurately?
opts: The bladder develops solely from intermediate mesoderm
The bladder and rectum arise from an identical final compartment
Cloacal origin is printed, but the primitive-rectum parenthesis needs correction
The entire bladder develops from primitive rectum
questions.exp: The scan says cloaca (primitive rectum). Bladder epithelium mainly arises from the vesical urogenital sinus after cloacal partition, not the primitive rectum; the parenthesis must not be taught as correct anatomy. (Book p717)

questions.q: The book traces the embryonic trigone to the ______ duct.
questions.exp: The book labels trigone mesonephric-duct/mesodermal in origin; distinguish this embryonic contribution from later epithelial remodelling. (Book p717)

questions.q: The embryology list assigns the prostate to which structure?
questions.exp: Prostate: primitive urogenital sinus. (Book p717)

questions.q: Up to the ejaculatory-duct opening, the prostatic urethra is assigned to the ______ canal.
questions.exp: The source prints vesico-ureteric canal; vesicourethral canal is the intended term in this embryology context. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which pair comes from the pelvic part of the definitive urogenital sinus?
questions.exp: Membranous urethra and remaining prostatic urethra: pelvic part of definitive urogenital sinus. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which correction is needed for the spongy-urethra origin line?
opts: Use mesonephric duct for the whole spongy urethra
Use metanephric blastema for urethral epithelium
Use phallic part, not the printed cephalic part
Use primitive rectum, not urogenital sinus
questions.exp: The line prints cephalic part. The intended embryological division is the phallic part of the urogenital sinus; the printed term is explicitly flagged. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which cloacal derivative gives rise to the rectum?
questions.exp: Rectum: primitive rectum derived from cloaca. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which pairing follows the book's two anal-canal bullets?
opts: Above: ureteric bud; below: anal pit
questions.exp: Anal canal up to the pectinate line: cloaca; below the line: anal pit. (Book p717)

questions.q: From outside inward, which regional sequence is labelled in the nephron figure?
questions.exp: Nephron figure labels cortex above the outer and inner medulla. (Book p717)

questions.q: The outer medulla is subdivided into outer and inner ______.
questions.exp: The figure divides outer medulla into outer stripe and inner stripe. (Book p717)

questions.q: Where is the medullary-ray callout placed in the nephron figure?
opts: In the renal pelvis beside a calyx
In the cortex alongside straight tubules
questions.exp: The medullary ray label points to straight tubular structures extending into cortex. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which figure-labelled loop extends farther into the inner medulla?
questions.exp: Long-loop nephron enters inner medulla; short-loop nephron turns higher in the outer-medullary region. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which origin chain is printed for the kidney's excretory part?
questions.exp: The excretory part is traced to nephrogenic cord from the urogenital ridge. (Book p717)

questions.q: Glomerulus plus Bowman's capsule is the renal ______.
questions.exp: Number 1: glomerulus plus Bowman's capsule form the renal corpuscle. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which segments are grouped under proximal tubule in the excretory tree?
questions.exp: Proximal tubule branches into proximal convoluted and proximal straight tubules. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which segment labels belong to pars convoluta in the book?
questions.exp: Number 2: proximal convoluted tubule, pars convoluta, S1 and S2. (Book p717)

questions.q: The proximal straight tubule or pars recta corresponds to segment ______.
questions.exp: Number 3: proximal straight tubule, pars recta, S3. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which pair forms the intermediate-tubule branch?
opts: Cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts
Thin descending and thin ascending limbs
Proximal convoluted and proximal straight tubules
Thick ascending and distal convoluted tubules
questions.exp: Intermediate tubule comprises numbered thin descending (4) and thin ascending (5) limbs. (Book p717)

questions.q: The thick ascending limb is also called the distal ______ tubule.
questions.exp: Number 6: thick ascending limb, also called distal straight tubule. (Book p717)

questions.q: Which numbered segment is the distal convoluted tubule in the source legend?
questions.exp: Number 7: distal convoluted tubule, the other distal-tubule branch. (Book p717)

questions.q: What name does the printed excretory legend give to number 8?
questions.exp: The legend prints macula densa at 8. The diagram is schematic; the macula densa is a specialised tubular plaque near the glomerular vascular pole, not a separate long tubular segment. (Book p717)

questions.q: Number 9 in the collecting-part legend is the ______ tubule.
questions.exp: Collecting legend 9: connecting tubule (CT). (Book p718)

questions.q: Which sequence identifies collecting-duct labels 10 → 11 → 12?
questions.exp: Collecting legend 10, 11, 12: cortical, outer medullary and inner medullary collecting ducts. (Book p718)

questions.q: Which structure is NOT included in the book's collecting-part bracket?
questions.exp: The collecting-part bracket lists CT, CD, ureter, pelvis and calyces. (Book p718)

questions.q: The collecting-part tree gives its epithelial origin as the ______ bud.
questions.exp: Collecting-part origin: epithelium of ureteric bud. (Book p718)

questions.q: Which chain continues backward from the ureteric bud in the source?
questions.exp: Ureteric bud derives from mesonephric duct, which derives from intermediate mesoderm. (Book p718)

questions.q: Which nephron-type pairing matches the table headings?
questions.exp: The table calls cortical nephrons short-looped and juxtamedullary nephrons long-looped. (Book p718)

questions.q: What cortical-to-juxtamedullary percentage split is printed?
questions.exp: Cortical nephrons make up 85%; juxtamedullary nephrons 15%. (Book p718)

questions.q: Which paired loop-tip locations follow the source table?
opts: Cortical: cortex only; juxtamedullary: renal sinus
Cortical: medullary junction; juxtamedullary: inner medulla
questions.exp: The short-loop tip is described at the outer/inner medullary junction; the long-loop tip lies inside inner medulla. (Book p718)

questions.q: Which nephron group has the major urine-concentrating role in the table?
questions.exp: Cortical nephrons have a lesser role in concentration; juxtamedullary nephrons have a major role. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: Renal function deteriorates over hours to days. Which label does this book flowchart use?
questions.exp: The flowchart labels this acute kidney injury. Clinical AKI diagnosis uses defined creatinine/urine-output criteria, not timing alone. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: Which two broad branches descend from AKI in this teaching diagram?
questions.exp: These are the branches shown, not an exhaustive classification of all AKI mechanisms. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: The first tubulointerstitial branch is acute tubular necrosis or tubular ______.
questions.exp: Acute tubular necrosis/tubular injury is the first tubulointerstitial branch. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: Which cause is marked most common under acute tubular injury?
questions.exp: The book identifies ischemia as the most common cause of acute tubular injury. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: The site marked most common for ischemic tubular injury is the proximal ______ tubule.
questions.exp: The most commonly affected site is PST, proximal straight tubule. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: Which mechanism is paired with acute interstitial nephritis in the source branch?
questions.exp: Acute interstitial nephritis is paired with hypersensitivity reaction. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: Which pair completes the flowchart's extrarenal AKI branch?
questions.exp: Causes outside the kidney divide into pre-renal and post-renal branches. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: A renal decline evolves over days to weeks rather than hours. Which source branch names this time course?
questions.exp: This is the book's time-course label, not a substitute for investigating the cause. (Book p718)

questions.sec: Applied aspect: approach to renal failure
questions.q: What change is listed under the CKD branch?
opts: Increased number of newly formed nephrons
questions.exp: CKD is expanded as chronic kidney disease and linked to decreased functional nephron number. (Book p718)

questions.q: Which ion is the explicit exception to the PCT maximum-reabsorption statement?
questions.exp: The book singles out magnesium. Its all-ions wording is a simplification, not a universal claim about every renal solute. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which pair is grouped under secondary active PCT transport?
questions.exp: PCT transporter tree: secondary active transport includes symport and antiport. (Book p719)

questions.q: The first PCT symporter couples sodium to ______ uptake.
questions.exp: Symport 1: sodium-dependent amino-acid transporter. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which transporter name is printed for sodium-coupled glucose uptake?
questions.exp: Symport 2: sodium-dependent glucose transporter, SGLT-2. (Book p719)

questions.q: The listed sodium-dependent phosphate transporter is type ______.
questions.exp: Symport 3: sodium-dependent phosphate transporter type II. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which exchange is listed under PCT antiport?
questions.exp: The secondary active antiport is sodium–hydrogen exchange. (Book p719)

questions.q: Passive paracellular transport occurs between two adjacent ______.
questions.exp: Passive transport is paracellular, on the boundary between two cells. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which interpretation preserves the phosphate-loss chain without repeating its overstatement?
opts: PCT damage can cause phosphate wasting and rickets; handling is not kidney-only
Phosphate is neither absorbed by gut nor stored in bone
PCT damage always prevents urinary phosphate loss
Rickets in this chain is caused by increased phosphate retention
questions.exp: The scan's only handled in kidney wording is inaccurate: intestine and bone also participate. Its local chain links PCT damage to urinary phosphate loss and rickets. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which group labels the three luminal sodium-coupled entries in the upper PCT cell?
questions.exp: Upper PCT figure luminal symports carry Na with amino acids, glucose and phosphate. (Book p719)

questions.q: How should the upper PCT figure's basolateral Na/H arrows be handled?
opts: Conclude that no luminal Na/H exchange occurs
Conclude that the PCT has no sodium gradients
Flag the sketch; the canonical apical Na/H exchanger is not relocated by it
Treat basolateral Na/H as the canonical PCT apical transporter
questions.exp: The upper sketch labels Na/H on the basolateral side; the lower sketch correctly depicts luminal exchange. Basolateral Na/K ATPase normally sustains the sodium gradient. This inconsistent drawing is not an authoritative replacement for physiology. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which is NOT among the solutes listed beside the PCT passive paracellular arrow?
questions.exp: The displayed list is water, calcium, sodium, magnesium and potassium. It identifies the figure labels, not equal transport fractions for each solute. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which direction is shown for the lower cell's luminal Na/H exchange?
opts: Both sodium and hydrogen enter the cell
Sodium enters; hydrogen leaves the cell
Hydrogen enters; sodium leaves the cell
Both sodium and hydrogen leave the cell
questions.exp: Lower PCT cell: luminal Na/H exchange brings sodium in and secretes hydrogen. (Book p719)

questions.q: Secreted hydrogen combines with luminal bicarbonate to form ______.
questions.exp: Luminal hydrogen combines with bicarbonate to form carbonic acid. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which enzyme and products belong to the luminal bicarbonate-recovery step?
opts: CA IV; water and carbon dioxide
questions.exp: Luminal carbonic anhydrase IV converts carbonic acid to water and carbon dioxide. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which product is drawn crossing into the lower PCT cell after luminal carbonic-acid breakdown?
questions.exp: The carbon-dioxide arrow crosses from lumen into the PCT cell. (Book p719)

questions.q: Inside the lower PCT cell, carbonic anhydrase type ______ participates in bicarbonate recovery.
questions.exp: Intracellular carbonic anhydrase II forms carbonic acid from water and carbon dioxide. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which paired fates complete the PCT bicarbonate diagram?
opts: Both ions are converted directly into glucose
Hydrogen recycles luminally; bicarbonate exits basolaterally
Bicarbonate exits luminally; hydrogen is trapped permanently
Both ions exit only through the ureter
questions.exp: Intracellular carbonic acid supplies recycled H+ and bicarbonate exiting basolaterally. (Book p719)

questions.q: Most renal magnesium reabsorption occurs in the ______ ascending limb of Henle.
questions.exp: The closing note locates maximum magnesium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb. (Book p719)

questions.q: Which distinction is needed when reading the page's Fanconi/proximal-RTA heading?
opts: Every proximal RTA necessarily includes all Fanconi solute losses
Fanconi syndrome is exclusively distal acidification failure
Proximal RTA always indicates normal bicarbonate reabsorption
Fanconi is generalised PCT dysfunction; proximal RTA can occur in isolation
questions.exp: The heading groups these terms, but isolated proximal bicarbonate wasting does not necessarily constitute full Fanconi syndrome. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which comparison sign is printed between inherited and acquired Fanconi causes?
questions.exp: This records the source's emphasis; relative frequencies depend on the population and age. (Book p720)

questions.q: A child has generalised proximal tubular losses. Which cause is labelled most common for this age in the book?
questions.exp: Cystinosis is labelled the most common childhood cause. (Book p720)

questions.q: Cystinosis is inherited in an autosomal ______ pattern.
questions.exp: Cystinosis is labelled autosomal recessive. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which metabolic disorder follows cystinosis in the inherited-cause list?
questions.exp: Galactosemia is the next inherited Fanconi cause. (Book p720)

questions.q: For an adolescent with Fanconi features, which cause receives the book's age-specific emphasis?
questions.exp: Wilson disease is marked most common in adolescents. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which acquired category is marked most common in adults?
questions.exp: Drugs are labelled the most common acquired cause in adults. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which drug is NOT in the first three entries of the acquired Fanconi drug list?
questions.exp: The adult drug list, first three entries: ifosfamide, tenofovir, valproate. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which pair completes the page's Fanconi-causing drug list?
questions.exp: The final drug entries are outdated tetracycline and cisplatin. (Book p720)

questions.q: An older adult develops Fanconi syndrome. Which disease is the book's most-common elderly association?
questions.exp: Multiple myeloma is marked most common in the elderly. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which pair is singled out for acidosis without generalised PCT dysfunction?
questions.exp: The source distinguishes their bicarbonate-reabsorption effect from generalised Fanconi losses; topiramate can cause mixed tubular acidification effects. (Book p720)

questions.q: Urinary phosphate loss in Fanconi syndrome can produce renal ______.
questions.exp: Cardinal feature 1: phosphorus loss causes renal rickets. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which statement appropriately qualifies the Fanconi RFT/proteinuria line?
opts: Minimal proteinuria excludes all tubular injury
Fanconi syndrome invariably requires dialysis at diagnosis
Normal RFT and little proteinuria do not guarantee absence of future CKD
Normal RFT proves that CKD can never develop
questions.exp: The book prints no risk for CKD. This is not universally correct: underlying disorders such as cystinosis can progress to CKD. Preserve the source claim as a flagged error, not reassurance. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which glucose pattern is characteristic of a proximal tubular reabsorptive defect?
questions.exp: Cardinal feature 3: euglycemic glycosuria. (Book p720)

questions.q: Wasting and growth retardation are linked to urinary loss of ______.
questions.exp: Cardinal feature 4: amino-acid loss in urine causes wasting/growth retardation. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which loss directly produces Fanconi-associated NAGMA?
questions.exp: Cardinal feature 5: urinary bicarbonate loss causes normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. (Book p720)

questions.q: What anion-gap interval is given with proximal-RTA NAGMA?
questions.exp: This is the source's reference interval; laboratory ranges depend on method and whether potassium is included. (Book p720)

questions.q: Normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis is also described as ______ acidosis.
questions.exp: NAGMA is also called hyperchloremic acidosis. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which function can remain intact in isolated proximal RTA after bicarbonate falls below its renal threshold?
opts: Normal glucose reabsorption in all Fanconi cases
Proximal bicarbonate recovery at all plasma levels
questions.exp: The book attributes preserved acidification to intercalated cells. Urine can be alkaline during bicarbonaturia and acidify after plasma bicarbonate falls. (Book p720)

questions.q: How should the printed urine-pH value 4–4.5 be interpreted?
opts: A diagnostic threshold excluding every form of RTA
A source-specific acidic value, not the full normal urinary pH range
The mandatory pH of every healthy urine sample
Proof that proximal RTA always has alkaline urine
questions.exp: Normal urine pH varies; minimum physiologic pH is roughly 4.5. Proximal RTA may acidify urine once bicarbonate is depleted; the printed range should not become a rigid diagnostic rule. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which serum bicarbonate range accompanies the book's relatively mild proximal-RTA acidosis description?
questions.exp: The source's no significant acidosis means relative to its distal-RTA comparison, not absence of metabolic acidosis or a guarantee of mild disease. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which ordered chain explains the salt-loss-associated potassium change in Fanconi syndrome?
opts: Volume loss → RAAS → aldosterone → K loss → hypokalemia
Volume gain → renin suppression → K retention → hypokalemia
Volume loss → aldosterone suppression → K retention → hypokalemia
Volume gain → RAAS suppression → K loss → hyperkalemia
questions.exp: Salt/water depletion → secondary RAAS activation → increased aldosterone → K wasting → hypokalemia. (Book p720)

questions.q: The urate abnormality listed under other Fanconi features is ______.
questions.exp: Other feature: hypouricemia. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which low circulating metabolite is listed immediately after hypouricemia?
questions.exp: Other feature: hypocarnitinemia. (Book p720)

questions.q: Increased urine volume in the other-features list is termed ______.
questions.exp: Other feature: polyuria. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which volume consequence appears in the right-hand other-features column?
questions.exp: Other feature: dehydration. (Book p720)

questions.q: How is proteinuria qualified in the final Fanconi feature bullet?
questions.exp: The source says minimal; proximal dysfunction may produce low-molecular-weight tubular proteinuria, and degree varies by cause. (Book p720)

questions.q: Which cell is NOT among the four categories in this CCD tree?
questions.exp: The fourth source category is an unnamed cell, discussed later. This is a teaching diagram, not a claim that ADH-responsive cells form a separate accepted cell lineage. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which orientation is used in the P-cell figure?
questions.exp: The P-cell figure marks luminal membrane left and basolateral membrane right. (Book p721)

questions.q: The adrenal zone supplying the P-cell hormone in the diagram is zona ______.
questions.exp: Zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone, which binds the depicted aldosterone receptor. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which signalling sequence does the P-cell sketch depict?
questions.exp: AIP is printed as aldosterone inducing protein; aldosterone-induced proteins is the usual interpretation. Mineralocorticoid receptors are intracellular despite the membrane-adjacent schematic symbol. (Book p721)

questions.q: The luminal sodium channel stimulated downstream of aldosterone is ______.
questions.exp: ENaC is a sodium channel. The sketch also draws water and H/K arrows around it; ENaC does not directly conduct water or exchange sodium for H/K. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which interpretation avoids overreading the ROMK/SOMK sketch?
opts: ROMK is primarily a bicarbonate exchanger
SOMK is the standard name for every renal H pump
ENaC directly pumps H in exchange for water
ROMK is a K channel; the drawn H arrow does not make it a proton pump
questions.exp: ROMK is the standard renal outer medullary K-channel label. SOMK is reproduced as a nonstandard source label, not given an invented expansion. Hydrogen secretion is primarily attributed to intercalated-cell transporters, not ROMK. (Book p721)

questions.q: A patient has hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis from excess aldosterone. Which syndrome labels this triad in the book?
questions.exp: The triad describes primary aldosteronism in this source; real patients may lack hypokalemia. (Book p721)

questions.q: Hypoaldosteronism is linked here to renal tubular acidosis type ______.
questions.exp: The pathology heading links hypoaldosteronism to type-IV RTA. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which potassium/renal-function pattern can point to hypoaldosteronism in the source?
opts: Normal potassium despite anuria in all cases
questions.exp: The first RTA-IV descriptor is hyperkalemia without renal failure. (Book p721)

questions.q: In someone with renal impairment, which potassium finding strengthens suspicion of RTA-IV?
opts: Hyperkalemia out of proportion to renal impairment
questions.exp: The second descriptor is hyperkalemia disproportionate to the degree and duration of renal failure. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which hormonal pattern defines hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism?
questions.exp: The low-renin true-hypoaldosteronism branch has reduced renin and reduced aldosterone. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which anti-inflammatory drug group is listed under hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism?
questions.exp: Low-renin cause 1: NSAIDs. (Book p721)

questions.q: The second low-renin drug category blocks ______ receptors.
questions.exp: Low-renin cause 2: beta-blockers. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which listed drug directly inhibits renin?
questions.exp: Low-renin cause 3: aliskiren, a direct renin inhibitor. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which diabetic mechanism is printed beneath the low-renin branch?
opts: Increased renal renin release in every case
questions.exp: Low-renin cause 4: diabetes, with autonomic neuropathy and beta-1 receptor dysfunction. (Book p721)

questions.q: The crossed conversion arrow beneath diabetes runs from prorenin to ______.
questions.exp: The diabetes subdiagram shows impaired prorenin-to-renin conversion. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which pattern belongs to hyper-reninemic hypoaldosteronism?
questions.exp: High-renin hypoaldosteronism means increased renin with reduced aldosterone. (Book p721)

questions.q: Renin is elevated but adrenal aldosterone production is deficient. Which named disease fits the source branch?
questions.exp: High-renin cause 1: adrenal insufficiency/Addison disease. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which pair is listed as RAAS-blocking causes in the high-renin branch?
questions.exp: High-renin drug list starts with ACE inhibitors and ARBs. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which drugs are grouped under impaired aldosterone synthesis in this flowchart?
questions.exp: The label is source grouping; these agents impair adrenal steroid/aldosterone production through different mechanisms, not necessarily selective aldosterone-synthase inhibition. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which pair is printed under chronic tubulointerstitial fibrosis in acquired PHA?
questions.exp: The source says vesico-urethral reflux; vesicoureteral reflux is the intended urinary reflux disorder. Both reflux-associated damage and obstruction can impair distal tubular responsiveness. (Book p721)

questions.q: The immunosuppressant group listed in this acquired-PHA branch is ______ inhibitors.
questions.exp: Calcineurin inhibitors can contribute to hyperkalemia and tubular dysfunction; the source places them under fibrosis, which is not their only mechanism. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which pair blocks mineralocorticoid receptors in the acquired-PHA list?
questions.exp: Aldosterone receptor blockers: spironolactone and eplerenone. (Book p721)

questions.q: Amiloride and triamterene directly block the ______ channel.
questions.exp: ENaC channel blockers: amiloride and triamterene. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which antibiotic follows ENaC blockers and is compared with triamterene?
questions.exp: The source compares it with triamterene; its clinically relevant amiloride-like ENaC inhibition can cause hyperkalemia. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which antimicrobial completes the acquired pseudo-hypoaldosteronism list?
questions.exp: Pentamidine is the final acquired drug listed. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which inherited PHA types are named at the far-right end of the tree?
questions.exp: Inherited pseudo-hypoaldosteronism branches are PHA type 1 and type 2. (Book p721)

questions.q: Which is NOT listed as a renin stimulus in the top-of-page note?
questions.exp: Renin stimulators: prostaglandins, beta-1 receptors and renal hypoperfusion. (Book p722)

questions.q: Which inhibitor-to-renin-stimulus pairing follows the diagram?
questions.exp: The side arrows show NSAIDs inhibiting prostaglandin signalling and beta-blockers inhibiting beta-1 signalling. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which transport direction is shown at the alpha-cell H/K ATPase?
questions.exp: Alpha-intercalated-cell black luminal symbol is H/K ATPase: H secreted and K taken into cell. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: The second alpha-cell luminal pump directly secretes ______.
questions.exp: The alpha-cell red luminal symbol is H ATPase. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: The enzyme labelled inside the alpha-intercalated cell is carbonic anhydrase ______.
questions.exp: The alpha-cell intracellular enzyme is carbonic anhydrase II. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which luminal movement is associated with pendrin in the beta-cell diagram?
questions.exp: Beta-cell luminal pendrin exchanges bicarbonate outward for chloride inward. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which interpretation of the beta-cell basolateral label is safest?
opts: Move luminal pendrin to the basolateral membrane
Conclude that beta cells only reabsorb bicarbonate
Record the anion-exchanger label but flag the simplified sketch
Treat the sketch as proof that no basolateral H pump exists
questions.exp: The scan labels anion exchanger/anions on the basolateral side. Standard beta-intercalated physiology emphasises basolateral H ATPase and apical pendrin; do not replace that physiology with this inconsistent sketch. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: The book's autosomal-dominant distal-RTA branch specifies an ______ defect.
questions.exp: Inherited distal-RTA AD branch: anion-exchanger defect. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which pump defects are grouped under inherited AR distal RTA in the source?
questions.exp: The source groups both pumps; established inherited distal-RTA genotypes require gene-specific interpretation rather than treating every H/K-pump defect as an equivalent common cause. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: A child has inherited distal RTA with an acid-secretory pump defect. Which extra-renal finding is flagged?
questions.exp: The inherited AR branch may present with sensorineural hearing loss. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which autoimmune disorder is labelled the most common acquired cause of distal RTA?
questions.exp: Acquired distal RTA: Sjogren syndrome is marked most common. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which pair is grouped as rare acquired distal-RTA agents?
questions.exp: Toluene is a solvent exposure, not a therapeutic drug despite the source's drugs heading. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which disease pair completes the rare acquired distal-RTA list?
questions.exp: The scan uses primary biliary cirrhosis; primary biliary cholangitis is the current name. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which age/RFT description opens the source's distal-RTA manifestations?
questions.exp: These are source generalisations, not exclusions: acquired distal RTA occurs in adults and renal function varies by cause. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which pH/time criterion is printed for inability to acidify urine?
questions.exp: This is the source description, not a stand-alone clinical diagnostic rule; interpret urine pH with systemic acidosis, infection, medication and collection context. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which serum bicarbonate interval is printed for significant distal-RTA acidosis?
questions.exp: Significant distal-RTA NAGMA: bicarbonate 10–12 mEq/L. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which change connects bone calcium mobilisation with the distal-RTA urinary findings?
questions.exp: The scan says calcium reabsorption from bone; resorption/mobilisation is the intended process. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: The stone type named in the distal-RTA calcium branch is calcium ______.
questions.exp: Hypercalciuria subbranch 1: calcium-phosphate stone formation. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Where is nephrocalcinosis located in this distal-RTA list?
questions.exp: Hypercalciuria subbranch 2: medullary nephrocalcinosis. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which skeletal outcome completes the calcium-loss subbranches?
questions.exp: Hypercalciuria subbranch 3: renal rickets. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Low urinary ______ is a separate stone-promoting feature of distal RTA.
questions.exp: Hypocitraturia leads to stones. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which causal chain finishes the distal-RTA clinical list?
opts: Salt retention → high perfusion → low aldosterone → low K
Salt loss → high perfusion → low aldosterone → high K
Salt retention → low perfusion → low aldosterone → high K
Salt loss → low perfusion → high aldosterone → low K
questions.exp: Salt/water wasting → reduced renal perfusion → secondary hyperaldosteronism → hypokalemia. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: The enzyme defect attached to type-III RTA is carbonic anhydrase ______.
questions.exp: Type-III RTA note: carbonic anhydrase II defect. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which correction is needed for the skeletal feature in the CA-II-deficiency note?
opts: The printed osteoporosis is synonymous with osteopetrosis
CA-II deficiency cannot have any skeletal findings
Classic association is osteopetrosis, not the printed osteoporosis
Classic association is rickets only, never osteopetrosis
questions.exp: The scan says osteoporosis. Carbonic-anhydrase-II deficiency classically causes osteopetrosis with RTA and cerebral calcification; the source wording is flagged, not silently adopted. (Book p722)

questions.sec: α-1 & β-1 cells and type-1/distal RTA
questions.q: Which neurologic pair completes the source's type-III RTA note?
questions.exp: The source uses outdated disability terminology; intellectual disability is used here. These findings are associated features, not mandatory in every patient. (Book p722)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: How should the table's shared AR inheritance and M>F statement be understood?
opts: A source generalisation, not a rule for every distal or proximal RTA
Proof that all RTA is inherited and affects only males
Proof that autosomal-dominant distal RTA cannot occur
Proof that normal RFT excludes all forms of RTA
questions.exp: The cell prints inherited cause (M>F), autosomal recessive and normal RFT. This conflicts with the preceding AD/acquired branches if applied universally; inheritance and sex distribution depend on cause. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which site pairing follows the distal-versus-proximal RTA table?
questions.exp: Defect-site row: distal alpha-intercalated cell; proximal global PCT dysfunction. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which transporter is NOT listed in the distal-RTA defect cell?
questions.exp: Distal defect row lists H ATPase, H/K ATPase and anion exchanger. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which group fills the proximal-RTA defect cell?
opts: Glomerular slit proteins and basement membrane
H ATPase, pendrin, aldosterone receptor only
questions.exp: This row describes generalised PCT dysfunction; isolated proximal RTA need not disrupt every listed transport route. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which urinary phosphate-loss comparison is printed?
questions.exp: Phosphorus-loss row: no in distal; significant in proximal. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which urinary calcium-loss comparison is printed?
questions.exp: This is the source's simplified comparison; actual urine calcium depends on etiology and treatment. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which rickets mechanism pairing follows the table?
opts: Distal: calcium loss; proximal: phosphate loss
Distal: phosphate loss; proximal: calcium loss
questions.exp: Rickets row: calcium loss in distal versus phosphorus loss in proximal. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: How does the table grade acidosis in distal versus proximal RTA?
questions.exp: This is a relative teaching comparison, not a severity guarantee for an individual case. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which secondary-hyperaldosteronism comparison does the table print?
questions.exp: Secondary hyperaldosteronism row: severe distal, mild proximal. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: The table grades distal hypokalemia as severe and proximal hypokalemia as ______.
questions.exp: Hypokalemia row: severe distal, mild proximal. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which urine amino-acid pattern is assigned to the proximal/Fanconi column?
opts: Both types always retain all amino acids
questions.exp: Aminoaciduria row: no in distal; significant in proximal. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which pairing matches the hypocitraturia row?
questions.exp: Hypocitraturia row: present distal, absent proximal. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which paired daily bicarbonate doses are printed for distal and proximal RTA, respectively?
questions.exp: These are source teaching ranges, not an individual prescription. Alkali therapy requires clinical assessment, potassium monitoring and dose titration. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: The hormone acting on the source's unnamed collecting-duct cells is ______.
questions.exp: Unnamed-cell hormone: ADH. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which channel family is named beneath ADH in the unnamed-cell section?
questions.exp: Unnamed-cell channel protein: aquaporin. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which correction is needed for the countercurrent-exchanger bullet?
opts: The loop of Henle has no concentrating role
Vasa recta perform exchange; collecting ducts respond to the gradient
Collecting ducts are the sole vascular countercurrent exchanger
Aquaporin converts collecting ducts into vasa recta
questions.exp: The printed attribution is retained as a source caveat. Countercurrent exchange belongs primarily to vasa recta; loop multiplication and collecting-duct water permeability are distinct processes. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: ADH-dependent aquaporin activity supports reabsorption of free ______.
questions.exp: The next function is reabsorption of free water. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which differential is used to introduce the urine anion gap?
questions.exp: VIPoma represents gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss in this example. The gap is an indirect ammonium surrogate and has limitations. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which urine electroneutrality equation is shown?
questions.exp: Electroneutrality: Na + K + unmeasured cations = Cl + unmeasured anions. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Urine anion gap is urine Na + K minus ______.
questions.exp: Rearranged urine gap: Na + K − Cl = unmeasured anions − unmeasured cations. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: With hyperchloremic acidosis, a positive urine anion gap suggests which source branch?
questions.exp: Interpret in context; unmeasured urinary anions, low urine sodium and other confounders can make the surrogate unreliable. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: A patient has secretory diarrhea and a negative urine anion gap during NAGMA. Which example fits the book?
questions.exp: A negative gap points toward VIPoma in the second branch. (Book p723)

questions.sec: RTA-1 vs RTA-2, un-named cells & urine anion gap
questions.q: Which diagram-labelled ion falls when renal acid excretion is impaired?
questions.exp: H+ combines with NH3 to form NH4+, an unmeasured urinary cation. Reduced NH4+ excretion explains the positive-gap tendency in distal RTA; not all proximal RTA has impaired distal ammonium excretion. (Book p723)

questions.q: TALH expands to the ______ ascending limb of Henle.
questions.exp: The section is the thick ascending limb of Henle, TALH. (Book p724)

questions.q: What ion stoichiometry is shown for luminal TALH cotransport?
questions.exp: Luminal transporter 1 brings Na, K and two Cl into the TALH cell. (Book p724)

questions.q: What does the luminal ROMK arrow contribute to TALH physiology?
questions.exp: Luminal transporter 2 is ROMK recycling potassium to create lumen electropositivity. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which correction is required for the TALH basolateral pump sketch?
opts: The pump exchanges 1 Na for 1 Cl only
Na/K ATPase exports 3 Na and imports 2 K, not the drawn 3 K
Na/K ATPase exports 2 Na and imports 3 K
The pump exports 3 Na and imports 3 K as a universal rule
questions.exp: The scan visibly labels 3 K and 3 Na. Standard Na/K ATPase stoichiometry is 3 Na out, 2 K in per ATP, so the potassium label is flagged. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which pair identifies the basolateral chloride channel and its accessory subunit?
questions.exp: The source writes ClCKB. ClC-Kb is a chloride channel; barttin is the accessory beta subunit of renal ClC-K channels. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which qualification is essential for the TALH claudin-arrow label?
opts: The H2O label proves freely permeable TALH water transport
Claudins transport only glucose and amino acids
The TALH has no paracellular divalent-cation transport
Ca/Mg paracellular transport is relevant, but TALH is water-impermeable
questions.exp: The source puts H2O with Ca/Mg on this arrow. Ca/Mg paracellular transport is appropriate; the water label conflicts with the thick ascending limb's water impermeability. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which transporter is highlighted under the initial Bartter defect bullet?
questions.exp: This describes NKCC2/type I; Bartter phenotypes involve several genes, as the page's later type branches imply. (Book p724)

questions.q: The Bartter transport defect produces severe renal salt ______.
questions.exp: The first causal arrow links the transport defect to severe salt wasting. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which paired consequences immediately follow severe salt wasting in the source?
questions.exp: Salt wasting produces polyuria and failure to thrive. (Book p724)

questions.q: The mediator named beside secondary RAAS activation in Bartter syndrome is ______.
questions.exp: Secondary RAAS activation is labelled prostaglandin mediated. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which ions are lost in urine downstream of the secondary RAAS branch?
questions.exp: The cascade next shows urinary K and H loss. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which paired blood abnormalities follow the K/H losses?
questions.exp: The first two consequence bullets are hypokalemia and alkalosis. (Book p724)

questions.q: The Bartter calcium-loss arrow leads from hypercalciuria to renal ______.
questions.exp: Hypercalciuria is linked to renal stones. (Book p724)

questions.q: How should the magnesium consequence bullet be interpreted?
opts: The printed 20% is a universal diagnostic requirement
It reports 20% hypomagnesemia, but its low-urine-Mg label needs caution
Low urinary Mg proves excessive urinary Mg loss by definition
All Bartter cases have obligatory severe hypermagnesemia
questions.exp: The source says hypomagnesuria → hypomagnesemia (20%). Renal magnesium wasting is not explained by a low absolute urinary label alone; assess urinary excretion relative to low serum Mg. The prevalence is source-specific. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which blood-pressure pattern is listed for Bartter syndrome?
questions.exp: The final Bartter consequence bullet is normal to low blood pressure. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which source Bartter type is marked most common, childhood-presenting and linked to maternal polyhydramnios?
questions.exp: This records the source's type-specific emphasis, not a universal prevalence claim across genetic cohorts. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which age group is printed under the type-II Bartter branch?
questions.exp: Type II branch: children. (Book p724)

questions.q: The Bartter branch labelled classical and adult is type ______.
questions.exp: Type III is called classical and linked to adult presentation. (Book p724)

questions.q: A Bartter phenotype is accompanied by sensorineural hearing loss. Which type is highlighted in the source?
questions.exp: Type IV may present with sensorineural hearing loss. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which inheritance does the book assign to its type-V Bartter branch?
questions.exp: This is the source's older classification; Bartter numbering is not uniform across contemporary genetic classifications. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which defect/finding pair completes the source's type-V branch?
questions.exp: The source associates an AD calcium-sensing receptor disorder with this older type-V label. Modern classification may reserve type V for MAGED2-related disease, so the label must remain source-qualified. (Book p724)

questions.q: Which mechanism explains indomethacin's place in the Bartter treatment diagram?
opts: Direct activation of ENaC increases salt loss
Direct inhibition of aquaporin corrects dehydration
Stimulation of renin prevents potassium loss
Prostaglandin inhibition reduces secondary RAAS drive
questions.exp: This is a mechanistic teaching point, not self-treatment advice; NSAID use in Bartter requires specialist monitoring of renal/GI risks and volume status. (Book p724)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: The apical DCT cotransporter couples sodium to ______.
questions.exp: DCT luminal physiology shows Na/Cl symport into the cell. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which basolateral transport arrangement is drawn for the DCT?
opts: Chloride exits; both sodium and potassium enter
Chloride enters; sodium enters while potassium exits
Chloride exits; sodium exits while potassium enters
Chloride enters; both sodium and potassium exit
questions.exp: The DCT diagram shows basolateral chloride exit above the sodium/potassium exchange arrows. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: The inheritance printed for Gitelman syndrome is autosomal ______.
questions.exp: Gitelman syndrome is listed as autosomal recessive. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which presentation age group is emphasised for Gitelman syndrome?
questions.exp: Adult presentation is the source emphasis; the condition can be recognised earlier. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which transporter defect underlies the Gitelman entry?
questions.exp: Gitelman defect: Na/Cl symport. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: How are renal-function tests described at the start of the Gitelman clinical list?
questions.exp: This is a usual source presentation, not a guarantee that renal function can never decline. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which sequence follows the less-salt-depletion Gitelman bullet?
opts: Salt loss → suppressed RAAS → respiratory acidosis alone
Salt retention → increased ADH → obligatory anuria
Salt loss → RAAS → mild low K/alkalosis with polyuria and poor growth
Salt retention → suppressed RAAS → hyperkalemia and edema
questions.exp: The source uses mild comparatively; hypokalemia and symptoms can be clinically important. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which qualification is needed for the TRMP6/ileum/100% chain?
opts: The source's 100% excludes any case without low Mg
Gitelman causes renal Mg wasting; a separate ileal defect is not obligatory
Every Gitelman case requires a proven ileal TRMP6 mutation
questions.exp: The scan writes TRMP6 (usually TRPM6), ileal impaired absorption and 100% hypomagnesemia. Gitelman is primarily SLC12A3/NCC-associated renal salt and magnesium wasting; do not require a second ileal mutation or universal low Mg. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which correction is needed for the no-hypocalciuria bullet?
opts: Gitelman typically has hypocalciuria; the printed no is misleading
Gitelman invariably has marked hypercalciuria and calcium stones
No stones proves that urinary calcium must be high
questions.exp: The line literally says no hypocalciuria. Typical Gitelman has low urine calcium and less calcium-stone/nephrocalcinosis tendency; the later table also lists less urine Ca. Stone absence is not guaranteed. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which magnesium state is explicitly negated in the next Gitelman bullet?
questions.exp: The following source bullet says no hypermagnesemia. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: What threshold is printed in the hypercalciuria note?
questions.exp: This is the source threshold, not a universal stand-alone criterion for all ages and collection settings. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which direction is printed in the polyuria comparison row?
questions.exp: Comparison row polyuria: more in Bartter, less in Gitelman. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: The comparison table lists greater polydipsia in ______ syndrome.
questions.exp: Comparison row polydipsia: more in Bartter, less in Gitelman. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which syndrome is assigned more dehydration in the table?
questions.exp: Comparison row dehydration: more in Bartter, less in Gitelman. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Tetany is especially prominent in a salt-wasting tubulopathy. Which side of this comparison table has more tetany?
questions.exp: Comparison row tetany: less in Bartter, more in Gitelman. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which growth-retardation comparison follows the printed table?
questions.exp: Comparison row growth retardation: more in Bartter, less in Gitelman. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which caveat applies to the salt-water-retention comparison row?
opts: Bartter prevents all renal sodium loss
Gitelman requires complete absence of urinary sodium
Retention is likely erroneous wording for the compared salt-wasting tendency
Both syndromes are primarily edematous salt-retaining disorders
questions.exp: The exact row says retention. Both syndromes are salt-wasting; the surrounding prose suggests depletion/wasting was intended. Do not silently convert the printed word into a true retention mechanism. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which urine-calcium comparison is printed?
questions.exp: Comparison row urine calcium: more Bartter, less Gitelman. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: The table gives greater nephrocalcinosis tendency to ______ syndrome.
questions.exp: Comparison row nephrocalcinosis: more Bartter, less Gitelman. (Book p725)

questions.sec: DCT & Gitelman syndrome; Bartter vs Gitelman
questions.q: Which reading handles the final magnesium row without concealing its ambiguity?
opts: Record Bartter 20%/type-V wording and flag Gitelman low versus earlier 100%
Treat low as proof that Gitelman rarely lowers magnesium
Treat 20% as a universal rate in every Bartter genotype
Ignore the prior Gitelman magnesium paragraph completely
questions.exp: The row labels hypomagnesemia: Bartter in 20% cases (type V Bartter), Gitelman low. Low could refer to Mg level rather than prevalence; the table and earlier 100% statement are not cleanly equivalent. Typical Gitelman hypomagnesemia remains the teaching point, with source-specific percentages and older Bartter classification flagged. (Book p725)
